data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: Timor-Leste uses the US dollar as its official currency, so it has no monetary policy at all; inflation is imported. It was volatile early on, 13.2% in 2011 on food prices, then low through the 2010s (with -1.5% in 2016), rising to 8.4% in 2023 on global shocks before easing to a projected 0.5% in 2025. Dollarization delivers price stability at the cost of any adjustment mechanism: when oil revenues fall, the entire adjustment lands on fiscal policy and the Petroleum Fund.
debt_management: Timor-Leste has almost no public debt: 0% through 2012, rising only to a projected 14.3% in 2025 as modest domestic borrowing began. The real balance sheet is the Petroleum Fund, which peaked above $19bn and has been drawn down heavily to fund budgets exceeding sustainable income; GDP is just $2.1bn projected for 2025. The fiscal question is not debt but fund depletion: at current withdrawal rates the fund faces exhaustion in the 2030s unless Greater Sunrise gas revenues materialize. Debt sustainability is irrelevant; fund sustainability is everything.

key_events.event: Political-military crisis; Australian-led intervention force deployed.
Assassination attempts on the president and PM; stability gradually restored.
UN mission ended; Timorese took full security responsibility.
Maritime boundary treaty with Australia settled Greater Sunrise revenue sharing.
COVID-19; Petroleum Fund drawdowns accelerated to fund the budget.
Parliamentary elections returned Xanana Gusmao's CNRT to power.

outlook_next_decade: Timor-Leste's outlook hinges on Greater Sunrise: if the gas field is developed, revenues extend the Petroleum Fund for decades; if not, the fund depletes and the state faces a fiscal cliff. Non-oil growth (coffee, tourism) is too small to fill the gap. Analytical assessment: the base case must assume continued large fund withdrawals with a hard deadline approaching; diversification has been promised for twenty years with little to show. Honest uncertainty about Sunrise timing dominates everything.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
